explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David, Israel's king, asks it right after calling the LORD his light, his salvation and his stronghold: “…whom shall I fear?” Then he asks a second one: “…whom shall I dread?” When the LORD is all of that to you, the question doesn't come with a list of names. I'd be standing there with a pencil and nothing to write.

David doesn't ask that one. His question in verse 1 is “…whom shall I fear?” Hiding does show up later, when he says the LORD will hide him in His shelter in the day of trouble (verse 5). Even then it's something he says will happen, not something he's asking. I'd be diving into the nearest cookie jar, I'll tell you that.

Close to a theme in this song, but not the question. Waiting comes at the very end, when David says to wait patiently for the LORD (verse 14), and he says it as a command. Up front, verse 1 asks “…whom shall I fear?” and “…whom shall I dread?” So he opens with courage and saves the waiting for last.

It's actually the other way around, friend. David says that when the wicked came upon him, his enemies and foes were the ones who stumbled and fell. David doesn't say he went down at all. The people who came to devour him ended up on the ground.

Right. Verse 2 says the wicked came upon David to devour his flesh, and then “…my enemies and foes stumbled and fell.” They were the ones who stumbled. I've tripped over my own mustache in the bakery, so I know the feeling, but they did it without any help from me.

That's it. David says, “though a war breaks out against me, I will keep my trust.” Notice the word is keep. Even if a war breaks out, he says he will hold onto it. I'd be holding onto my cookie box with both mustache ends.

David doesn't say that. Though an army encamps around him, he says his heart will not fear, and though a war breaks out, he will keep his trust (verse 3). Keeping his distance might sound sensible, but that's not what the song says. What he says he'll keep is his trust.

No sword in this verse. David doesn't say what he'll grab. He says what he'll keep, and it's his trust. A sword can be taken from you in a war, but David is talking about something he holds onto inside, so the answer is trust.

explanations.answer: To dwell in the LORD's house all his days
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David says, “One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life…” He's just talked about armies and wars, and his one ask is still to be near the LORD. I think that tells you where his heart was sitting.

explanations.answer: To see every one of his enemies defeated
explanations.explanation: David has just mentioned enemies, so I see why that tempts. But his one ask is something else. He wants to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of his life (verse 4). Enemies stumbling in verse 2 is something he remembers, not the thing he's asking for.

explanations.answer: To live a long and peaceful life in his land
explanations.explanation: That one's close on the "…all the days of my life…" part, but it's aimed at the wrong place. David doesn't ask for a peaceful life in his land. He asks to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of his life (verse 4). His one ask is about where he wants to be, and that's with the LORD.
Yep. Verse 4 says he wants “…to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and seek Him in His temple.” Gazing means looking, and not a quick glance either. David wants to stay and take it all in.

This one's true, friend. David says he wants to dwell in the LORD's house, “…to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and seek Him in His temple.” It's all right there in verse 4. He's not just visiting, he's looking at the LORD's beauty and seeking Him.
That's right. David says, “For in the day of trouble He will hide me in His shelter…” He says it as something he already knows will happen. I bet that kind of certainty lets a person sleep.

explanations.answer: Send an army to fight for him
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say that here. He does mention an army, but it's the one camped around him in verse 3. For the day of trouble, verse 5 says the LORD will hide him in His shelter. David's picture is of being kept safe, not of a battle.

explanations.answer: Bring down fire on his enemies
explanations.explanation: No fire in this verse. David says what the LORD will do for him, not what He'll do to his enemies. In the day of trouble, the LORD will hide him in His shelter (verse 5). It's a quiet picture, like being tucked away somewhere safe.
You got it. Verse 5 says, “He will set me high upon a rock.” So David has the shelter, the cover of the tent, and then he's lifted up on a rock. I'd say that's the LORD going all the way.
David doesn't say cave. The text says the LORD will set him high upon a rock. Going deep down would be the opposite direction. David's picture is of being lifted up (verse 5).

The city gates don't show up in this song. After the shelter and the cover of the tent, verse 5 says the LORD “…will set me high upon a rock.” David's talking about being lifted high, not about being walled in.
That's what he says. Verse 6 begins, “Then my head will be held high above my enemies around me.” Notice it follows the rock in verse 5. He's lifted up first, and then his head is held high.

It's true, friend. David says, “Then my head will be held high above my enemies around me.” That comes right after the LORD sets him high upon a rock in verse 5. His enemies are still around him, but his head is above them.

explanations.answer: Offer sacrifices with shouts of joy
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 6 says, “At His tabernacle I will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy…” That's shouts, plural, not a polite clap. The man I'd call loud is David, and I say that as a stamper who has been told to use his indoor voice.

explanations.answer: Hang up his sword and his armor
explanations.explanation: David doesn't mention a sword or armor in this verse. What he says is that he'll offer sacrifices at the LORD's tabernacle with shouts of joy (verse 6). Nothing in the text says he's putting anything down. He's lifting his voice up.

explanations.answer: Bow down in silence and weep
explanations.explanation: That's not the sound of this verse. David says he'll offer sacrifices at the tabernacle “…with shouts of joy…” and then he'll sing and make music to the LORD (verse 6). Quiet isn't the plan here. It's joy, out loud.
Yes. David says, “My heart said, ‘Seek His face.’” His heart is the one talking here, and what it says is to seek the LORD's face. David is listening to it.
That's not what his heart says. Verse 8 says, “My heart said, ‘Seek His face.’” There's no running in this verse. His heart points him toward the LORD.
No altar in this verse. David's heart says, “Seek His face.” and David answers, “Your face, O LORD, I will seek.” (verse 8). It's a seeking, not a building. His heart wants the LORD Himself.

It's the opposite, baker. David has just said he's seeking the LORD's face, so verse 9 asks, “Hide not Your face from me…” He wants the LORD to keep His face turned toward him. He's not asking Him to hide it.
That's right. In verse 9 David says, “Hide not Your face from me, nor turn away Your servant in anger.” He's been saying he will seek the LORD's face. He doesn't want it hidden.

Right. David says, “You have been my helper; do not leave me or forsake me, O God of my salvation.” He starts with what the LORD has been to him and then asks Him to keep being it. That makes sense to me, because the best helpers I know are the ones who stay.
David doesn't say that here. He calls the LORD his helper, and then he asks, “do not leave me or forsake me…” (verse 9). It's about being left alone. Tests aren't in this verse.

Neither one shows up in verse 9. After calling the LORD his helper, David says, “do not leave me or forsake me, O God of my salvation.” That's the request in that verse. Being humbled or broken isn't in it.

That's the word. David says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.” It's two sides in one line: forsake on one side, receive on the other. I think that's a verse for anybody who's felt left out of the group chat.
Not in this verse. David says that though his father and mother forsake him, “…the LORD will receive me.” (verse 10). Receive means He takes him in. Correcting isn't what David's talking about.
That's not the word. Verse 10 says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.” Even if the closest people leave, the LORD receives him. David isn't talking about a test.

That's what he says. Verse 11 reads, “Teach me Your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path, because of my oppressors.” The oppressors are the reason for the level path. David is asking to be taught and led with them in mind.

It's true, baker. David says, “Teach me Your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path, because of my oppressors.” That last part is the reason right there in the verse. He asks to be led because of the ones oppressing him.
That's right. David says, “…for false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence.” A witness is supposed to tell what happened, and these ones are false. I think that would sting.

David doesn't name them here. He names who is rising up against him in verse 12: “…false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence.” These are people speaking against him, not a nation he names.
David doesn't say that in this verse. Verse 12 says, “…false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence.” He names false witnesses, and nobody in his family is mentioned there.

That's the word. David says, “Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.” Just before this, he talks about false witnesses breathing out violence (verse 12). I love that word certain.

That's not the word. Verse 13 says, “Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.” David has just talked about people against him, so judgment seems possible. But the thing he's certain he'll see is the LORD's goodness.

David doesn't say wrath. He says he's certain to see “…the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.” (verse 13). That's what the word Still turns toward. After all those enemies, he looks for goodness.

Yes. The song ends, “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” He says it twice, and I think he means it. Waiting is hard for me, and I used to do it in a drawer.

explanations.answer: Lift your hands to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Not in this song's last verse. David ends with, “Wait patiently for the LORD…” (verse 14). That's the command, and he says it twice. Lifted hands aren't mentioned.

explanations.answer: Go out and fight for the LORD
explanations.explanation: David doesn't end with a call to fight. Verse 14 says, “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” The command is to wait, and he says it at the start and the end of the verse.

That's it. Verse 14 says, “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” So the strong and courageous part sits right in the middle of the waiting. That's a nice bookend for a song that began with “…whom shall I fear?”
That's not what David says. Between his two calls to wait, he says, “be strong and courageous.” Silent and calm aren't in verse 14.

Those words aren't in this verse. Verse 14 says, “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” In the middle of the waiting, David says to be strong and courageous.
